claim: Ryanodine receptors (RyRs) exhibit dynamic arrangements in cardiomyocytes.
source: Ryanodine receptors (RyRs) exhibit dynamic arrangements in cardiomyocytes, and we previously showed that 'dispersion' of RyR clusters disrupts Ca2+ homeostasis during heart failure (HF) (Kolstad et al., eLife, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references a previous publication (Kolstad et al., eLife, 2018).

claim: Dispersion of RyR clusters disrupts Ca2+ homeostasis during heart failure.
source: Ryanodine receptors (RyRs) exhibit dynamic arrangements in cardiomyocytes, and we previously showed that 'dispersion' of RyR clusters disrupts Ca2+ homeostasis during heart failure (HF) (Kolstad et al., eLife, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Kolstad et al., eLife, 2018).

claim: Treatment of healthy rat cardiomyocytes with isoproterenol for 1 hr triggered progressive fragmentation of RyR clusters.
source: We observed that treatment of healthy rat cardiomyocytes with isoproterenol for 1 hr triggered progressive fragmentation of RyR clusters.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CaMKII reversed isoproterenol-induced RyR cluster dispersion.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) reversed these effects, while cluster dispersion was reproduced by specific activation of CaMKII, and in mice with constitutively active Ser2814-RyR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: RyR cluster dispersion was reproduced by specific activation of CaMKII.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) reversed these effects, while cluster dispersion was reproduced by specific activation of CaMKII, and in mice with constitutively active Ser2814-RyR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: RyR cluster dispersion was observed in mice with constitutively active Ser2814-RyR.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) reversed these effects, while cluster dispersion was reproduced by specific activation of CaMKII, and in mice with constitutively active Ser2814-RyR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PKA activation promotes RyR cluster fragmentation.
source: A similar role of protein kinase A (PKA) in promoting RyR cluster fragmentation was established by employing PKA activation or inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Progressive cluster dispersion was linked to declining Ca2+ spark fidelity and magnitude.
source: Progressive cluster dispersion was linked to declining Ca2+ spark fidelity and magnitude, and slowed release kinetics from Ca2+ propagation between more numerous RyR clusters.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and modeling results in Figure 5.

claim: Progressive cluster dispersion was linked to slowed release kinetics from Ca2+ propagation between more numerous RyR clusters.
source: Progressive cluster dispersion was linked to declining Ca2+ spark fidelity and magnitude, and slowed release kinetics from Ca2+ propagation between more numerous RyR clusters.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and modeling results in Figure 5.

claim: In healthy cells, RyR dispersion served to dampen the stimulatory actions of β-adrenergic stimulation over the longer term.
source: In healthy cells, this served to dampen the stimulatory actions of β-adrenergic stimulation over the longer term and protect against pro-arrhythmic Ca2+ waves.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced Ca2+ wave incidence after prolonged isoproterenol treatment (Figure 4m).

claim: RyR dispersion in healthy cells protects against pro-arrhythmic Ca2+ waves.
source: In healthy cells, this served to dampen the stimulatory actions of β-adrenergic stimulation over the longer term and protect against pro-arrhythmic Ca2+ waves.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced Ca2+ wave incidence after prolonged isoproterenol treatment (Figure 4m).

claim: During heart failure, RyR dispersion was linked to impaired Ca2+ release.
source: However, during HF, RyR dispersion was linked to impaired Ca2+ release.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from heart failure cardiomyocytes shown in Figure 6.

claim: RyR localization and function are intimately linked via channel phosphorylation by both CaMKII and PKA.
source: Thus, RyR localization and function are intimately linked via channel phosphorylation by both CaMKII and PKA, which, while finely tuned in healthy cardiomyocytes, underlies impaired cardiac function during pathology.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Sarcolemmal depolarization triggers an influx of Ca2+ through voltage-gated L-type Ca2+ channels (LTCCs) within t-tubules.
source: Sarcolemmal depolarization triggers an influx of Ca2+ through voltage-gated L-type Ca2+ channels (LTCCs) within t-tubules, which in turn elicits a much larger release of Ca2+ into the cytosol via ryanodine receptors (RyRs) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cardiac excitation-contraction coupling.

claim: Ca2+ influx through LTCCs elicits a much larger release of Ca2+ into the cytosol via ryanodine receptors (RyRs) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
source: Sarcolemmal depolarization triggers an influx of Ca2+ through voltage-gated L-type Ca2+ channels (LTCCs) within t-tubules, which in turn elicits a much larger release of Ca2+ into the cytosol via ryanodine receptors (RyRs) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cardiac excitation-contraction coupling.

claim: Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR) depends on the precise organization of LTCCs and RyRs within dyadic junctions.
source: This process of Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR) depends on the precise organization of LTCCs and RyRs within dyadic junctions of the two membranes, with LTCCs located in nanoscale apposition to RyRs across the dyadic cleft (Bers, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature (Bers, 2001).

claim: RyRs are intrinsically organized into discrete clusters.
source: Intrinsically, RyRs are organized into discrete clusters, and these arrangements are thought to be critical in defining channel function.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: RyR cluster arrangements are critical in defining channel function.
source: Intrinsically, RyRs are organized into discrete clusters, and these arrangements are thought to be critical in defining channel function.
evidence: This is supported by inference from the literature and the current study's findings.

claim: RyR clusters located within close proximity are proposed to cooperatively operate as Ca2+ release units (CRUs) to generate Ca2+ sparks.
source: Indeed, RyR clusters located within close proximity are proposed to cooperatively operate as Ca2+ release units (CRUs) to generate Ca2+ sparks (Baddeley et al., 2009; Sobie et al., 2006), the elementary units of SR Ca2+ release (Cheng et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Baddeley et al., 2009; Sobie et al., 2006; Cheng et al., 1993).

claim: Ca2+ sparks are the elementary units of SR Ca2+ release.
source: Indeed, RyR clusters located within close proximity are proposed to cooperatively operate as Ca2+ release units (CRUs) to generate Ca2+ sparks (Baddeley et al., 2009; Sobie et al., 2006), the elementary units of SR Ca2+ release (Cheng et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Cheng et al., 1993).

claim: Contractile dysfunction and arrhythmogenesis are hallmarks of heart failure.
source: Contractile dysfunction and arrhythmogenesis are hallmarks of heart failure (HF), and considerable data have linked these phenomena to t-tubule disruption in this condition (Fowler et al., 2020; Louch et al., 2006; Orchard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Fowler et al., 2020; Louch et al., 2006; Orchard et al., 2013).

claim: Contractile dysfunction and arrhythmogenesis in heart failure have been linked to t-tubule disruption.
source: Contractile dysfunction and arrhythmogenesis are hallmarks of heart failure (HF), and considerable data have linked these phenomena to t-tubule disruption in this condition (Fowler et al., 2020; Louch et al., 2006; Orchard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Fowler et al., 2020; Louch et al., 2006; Orchard et al., 2013).

claim: RyR dispersion in failing cardiomyocytes specifically included fragmentation of RyR groupings into more numerous, smaller clusters, without any change in overall channel number.
source: This RyR rearrangement specifically included fragmentation of RyR groupings into more numerous, smaller clusters, without any change in overall channel number (Kolstad et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Kolstad et al., 2018).

claim: RyR dispersion was critically linked to low-fidelity spark generation.
source: RyR dispersion was critically linked to low-fidelity spark generation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Kolstad et al., 2018) and data in the current study.

claim: When Ca2+ release was successfully triggered by a CRU, propagation of Ca2+ between multiple clusters generated sparks with slow kinetics.
source: Furthermore, when Ca2+ release was successfully triggered by a CRU, propagation of Ca2+ between multiple clusters generated sparks with slow kinetics, and the overall Ca2+ transient was desychronized (Kolstad et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Kolstad et al., 2018) and data in the current study.

claim: RyR dispersion resulted in desynchronized overall Ca2+ transients.
source: Furthermore, when Ca2+ release was successfully triggered by a CRU, propagation of Ca2+ between multiple clusters generated sparks with slow kinetics, and the overall Ca2+ transient was desychronized (Kolstad et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Kolstad et al., 2018) and data in the current study.

claim: Similar fragmentation of CRUs has been reported in a sheep model of persistent atrial fibrillation.
source: Similar fragmentation of CRUs has been reported in a sheep model of persistent atrial fibrillation (Macquaide et al., 2015) and in monocrotaline-induced right ventricular failure in rats (Sheard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Macquaide et al., 2015).

claim: CRU fragmentation has been reported in monocrotaline-induced right ventricular failure in rats.
source: Similar fragmentation of CRUs has been reported in a sheep model of persistent atrial fibrillation (Macquaide et al., 2015) and in monocrotaline-induced right ventricular failure in rats (Sheard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Sheard et al., 2019).

claim: Nanoscale RyR positioning is fine-tuned by phosphorylation of the channels.
source: Previous work has indicated that nanoscale RyR positioning is fine-tuned by phosphorylation of the channels, at least acutely (Asghari et al., 2014; Asghari et al., 2020), and that both Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII)- and protein kinase A (PKA)-dependent phosphorylation of RyR disrupt its function during HF (Ling et al., 2009; Marx et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Asghari et al., 2014; Asghari et al., 2020).

claim: CaMKII-dependent phosphorylation of RyR disrupts its function during heart failure.
source: Previous work has indicated that nanoscale RyR positioning is fine-tuned by phosphorylation of the channels, at least acutely (Asghari et al., 2014; Asghari et al., 2020), and that both Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII)- and protein kinase A (PKA)-dependent phosphorylation of RyR disrupt its function during HF (Ling et al., 2009; Marx et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Ling et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2003).

claim: PKA-dependent phosphorylation of RyR disrupts its function during heart failure.
source: Previous work has indicated that nanoscale RyR positioning is fine-tuned by phosphorylation of the channels, at least acutely (Asghari et al., 2014; Asghari et al., 2020), and that both Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII)- and protein kinase A (PKA)-dependent phosphorylation of RyR disrupt its function during HF (Ling et al., 2009; Marx et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Marx et al., 2000).

claim: Prolonged β-adrenergic stimulation promotes RyR dispersion via both CaMKII- and PKA-dependent phosphorylation of the channel.
source: We demonstrate that prolonged β-adrenergic stimulation, as is well known to occur in HF, promotes RyR dispersion via both CaMKII- and PKA-dependent phosphorylation of the channel.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: RyR reorganization and sensitization are associated with a time-dependent increase in Ca2+ leak.
source: This RyR reorganization and sensitization are associated with a time-dependent increase in Ca2+ leak, slowing of Ca2+ spark kinetics, and reduced Ca2+ transient magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: RyR reorganization and sensitization are associated with slowing of Ca2+ spark kinetics.
source: This RyR reorganization and sensitization are associated with a time-dependent increase in Ca2+ leak, slowing of Ca2+ spark kinetics, and reduced Ca2+ transient magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: RyR reorganization and sensitization are associated with reduced Ca2+ transient magnitude.
source: This RyR reorganization and sensitization are associated with a time-dependent increase in Ca2+ leak, slowing of Ca2+ spark kinetics, and reduced Ca2+ transient magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Sufficiently dispersed RyRs inhibit the development of Ca2+ waves that underlie arrhythmia.
source: Indeed, we observed that sufficiently dispersed RyRs inhibit the development of Ca2+ waves that underlie arrhythmia.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4m.

claim: Blocking hyperphosphorylation of RyRs reverses channel dispersion in HF cells.
source: Conversely, blocking hyperphosphorylation of RyRs reverses channel dispersion in HF cells and associated impairment of Ca2+ release, providing new insight into the protective mechanisms of β-blockade in this disease.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Blocking hyperphosphorylation of RyRs reverses associated impairment of Ca2+ release in HF cells.
source: Conversely, blocking hyperphosphorylation of RyRs reverses channel dispersion in HF cells and associated impairment of Ca2+ release, providing new insight into the protective mechanisms of β-blockade in this disease.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Following 30 min of isoproterenol treatment, RyR cluster size significantly decreased.
source: However, after 30 min of isoproterenol treatment, RyR cluster size significantly decreased (Figure 1b), while cluster density increased (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Following 30 min of isoproterenol treatment, RyR cluster density increased.
source: However, after 30 min of isoproterenol treatment, RyR cluster size significantly decreased (Figure 1b), while cluster density increased (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: By 1 hr of β-AR activation, continued RyR rearrangement was sufficient to reduce CRU size.
source: By 1 hr of β-AR activation, continued RyR rearrangement was sufficient to reduce CRU size as fewer RyRs remained within clusters located ≤ 100 nm from their neighbors (Figure 1c, see enlargements in Figure 1a for representative images of CRUs).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Overall RyR density was unchanged by isoproterenol treatment.
source: Since overall RyR density was unchanged by isoproterenol treatment (Figure 1e), the detected differences in RyR organization did not result from channel degradation, but rather indicate progressive dispersion of RyR clusters into more numerous, smaller groupings.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The detected differences in RyR organization did not result from channel degradation.
source: Since overall RyR density was unchanged by isoproterenol treatment (Figure 1e), the detected differences in RyR organization did not result from channel degradation, but rather indicate progressive dispersion of RyR clusters into more numerous, smaller groupings.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that overall RyR density was unchanged.

claim: Similar proportions of clusters were characterized as dyadic under control conditions and following 60 min isoproterenol.
source: Based on these analyses, the majority of RyR clusters were classified as dyadic, and this proportion was observed to be similar under control and isoproterenol treatment conditions (83 ± 1.6% and 84 ± 1.0%, respectively; Figure 1g).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: RyR cluster dispersion was found to be restricted to RyRs within dyads.
source: Importantly, RyR cluster dispersion was found to be restricted to RyRs within dyads (control: 9.0 ± 0.5 vs. 60 min isoproterenol: 6.7 ± 0.4 RyRs/cluster, Figure 1h).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The organization of surface RyR clusters associated with the cardiomyocyte sarcolemma was largely unaffected by β-AR activation.
source: It should be noted that the above analyses were performed on RyR clusters within the cell interior. Interestingly, the organization of surface RyR clusters associated with the cardiomyocyte sarcolemma was largely unaffected by β-AR activation save for a slight increase (p=0.092) in cluster size following 10 min isoproterenol treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that RyR dispersion is a phenomenon restricted to internal, dyadic RyRs.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: RyR dispersion is a phenomenon restricted to internal, dyadic RyRs.
source: It should be noted that the above analyses were performed on RyR clusters within the cell interior. Interestingly, the organization of surface RyR clusters associated with the cardiomyocyte sarcolemma was largely unaffected by β-AR activation save for a slight increase (p=0.092) in cluster size following 10 min isoproterenol treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that RyR dispersion is a phenomenon restricted to internal, dyadic RyRs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that surface RyR clusters were largely unaffected by β-AR activation.

claim: A substantial portion of β-AR signaling is mediated via CaMKII.
source: In cardiomyocytes, it is well established that a substantial portion of β-AR signaling is mediated via CaMKII (Grimm and Brown, 2010) and includes CaMKII-mediated phosphorylation of RyRs (Ferrero et al., 2007; Grimm et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Grimm and Brown, 2010).

claim: β-AR signaling includes CaMKII-mediated phosphorylation of RyRs.
source: In cardiomyocytes, it is well established that a substantial portion of β-AR signaling is mediated via CaMKII (Grimm and Brown, 2010) and includes CaMKII-mediated phosphorylation of RyRs (Ferrero et al., 2007; Grimm et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Ferrero et al., 2007; Grimm et al., 2015).

claim: Increased RyR phosphorylation at the CaMKII site ser-2814 was particularly prominent during early stages of isoproterenol treatment.
source: Indeed, using flow cytometry analysis, we observed increased RyR phosphorylation at the CaMKII site ser-2814 that was particularly prominent during early stages of isoproterenol treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of AIP markedly reversed cluster dispersion induced by isoproterenol.
source: We found that the addition of AIP markedly reversed cluster dispersion (Figure 2a). This was reflected by a significant increase in both RyR cluster size (Figure 2d) and CRU size (Figure 2e), as well as a significant reduction in RyR cluster density (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2a, d, e, and f.

claim: Direct activation of CaMKII through the Epac2 pathway using 8-CPT-cAMP consistently reproduced the RyR cluster dispersion observed during isoproterenol stimulation.
source: Direct activation of CaMKII through the Epac2 pathway using 8-CPT-cAMP (10 µM) (Pereira et al., 2013) also consistently reproduced the RyR cluster dispersion observed during isoproterenol stimulation (Figure 2b, quantification in Figure 2d–f).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2b, d, e, and f.

claim: Caffeine application gave rise to significant reductions in both RyR cluster and CRU size, as well as a significant increase in cluster density.
source: We found that caffeine application gave rise to significant reductions in both RyR cluster and CRU size, as well as a significant increase in cluster density (Figure 2c, quantification in Figure 2d–f).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2c, d, e, and f.

claim: The RyR arrangement in the phosphomimetic S2814D mutant cells at baseline resembled the fragmented RyR organization observed in wildtype animals after isoproterenol treatment.
source: We found that the RyR arrangement in the phosphomimetic S2814D mutant cells at baseline resembled the fragmented RyR organization observed in wildtype (WT) animals after isoproterenol treatment (Figure 2g and h).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2g and h.

claim: Application of isoproterenol to S2814D cardiomyocytes did not lead to significant additional RyR dispersion.
source: Furthermore, application of isoproterenol to S2814D cardiomyocytes did not lead to significant additional RyR dispersion, and only tendencies toward smaller cluster and CRU sizes (Figure 2h and j–l).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2h, j, k, and l.

claim: Cardiomyocytes from non-phosphorylatable S2814A mutant mice exhibited similar RyR organization as in WT mice at baseline.
source: In contrast, cardiomyocytes from non-phosphorylatable S2814A mutant mice exhibited similar RyR organization as in WT mice at baseline (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Administering isoproterenol to S2814A cardiomyocytes promoted a significant reduction in cluster size and increased cluster density.
source: Administering isoproterenol to this group promoted a significant reduction in cluster size (Figure 2j) and increased cluster density (Figure 2l).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2j and l.

claim: β-AR-induced cluster dispersion was reversed by the addition of the PKA inhibitor H89.
source: Indeed, β-AR-induced cluster dispersion was reversed by the addition of the PKA inhibitor H89 (Figure 3a), as reflected by significantly increased cluster size (Figure 3c) and CRU size (Figure 3d), and reduced cluster density (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3a, c, d, and e.

claim: 6MB-cAMP treatment prompted RyR dispersion comparable to that elicited by isoproterenol.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3b, 6MB-cAMP treatment prompted RyR dispersion comparable to that elicited by isoproterenol.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: 6MB induced RyR dispersion in S2814A cardiomyocytes, which was comparable to that observed in WT.
source: Importantly, 6MB induced RyR dispersion in S2814A cardiomyocytes (Figure 3f and h–j), which was comparable to that observed in WT.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3f, h, i, and j.

claim: Dispersion observed in S2814A cardiomyocytes treated with isoproterenol was reversed by the addition of H89.
source: Similarly, dispersion observed in S2814A cardiomyocytes treated with isoproterenol was reversed by the addition of H89 (Figure 3g–j).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3g, h, i, and j.

claim: Spark frequency was augmented throughout the isoproterenol treatment period.
source: We observed that while spark frequency was augmented throughout the isoproterenol treatment period (Figure 4c), there was indeed a progressive slowing of both spark rise time (Figure 4d) and duration (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: There was a progressive slowing of both spark rise time and duration during isoproterenol treatment.
source: We observed that while spark frequency was augmented throughout the isoproterenol treatment period (Figure 4c), there was indeed a progressive slowing of both spark rise time (Figure 4d) and duration (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4d and e.

claim: Increased overall spark geometry during prolonged isoproterenol treatment was linked to progressively augmented Ca2+ leak.
source: Increased overall spark geometry (Figure 4f and g) during prolonged isoproterenol treatment was linked to progressively augmented Ca2+ leak, as calculated based on spark mass and frequency (Figure 4h).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4f, g, and h.

claim: Reversal of RyR dispersion by co-incubation of cells with either AIP or H89 after the initial isoproterenol treatment also reversed slowing of spark kinetics and isoproterenol-induced Ca2+ leak.
source: Importantly, reversal of RyR dispersion by co-incubation of cells with either AIP or H89 after the initial isoproterenol treatment also reversed slowing of spark kinetics and isoproterenol-induced Ca2+ leak (Figure 4d, e and h).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4d, e, and h.

claim: Isoproterenol treatment acutely increased Ca2+ transient magnitude; however, this reversed with continued exposure.
source: As expected, isoproterenol treatment acutely increased Ca2+ transient magnitude; however, this reversed with continued exposure (Figure 4j).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Ca2+ release tended to be more synchronous at early stages of isoproterenol treatment.
source: Similar changes were observed in the synchrony of Ca2+ release across the cell. Ca2+ release tended to be more synchronous at early stages of isoproterenol treatment (Figure 4l), in agreement with previous work indicating that increasing SR Ca2+ content and RyR sensitization enable more homogeneous Ca2+ transients (Brette et al., 2004; Øyehaug et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4l and citations to previous work (Brette et al., 2004; Øyehaug et al., 2013).

claim: After prolonged β-AR stimulation, RyR dispersal slowed Ca2+ spark kinetics, and declining SR content was coupled to a reversal of the synchronization of Ca2+ release observed at earlier time points.
source: However, after prolonged β-AR stimulation, RyR dispersal slowed Ca2+ spark kinetics, and declining SR content was coupled to a reversal of the synchronization of Ca2+ release observed at earlier time points (Figure 4l) and a modest slowing of the rising phase of the transient (Figure 4k).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4k and l.

claim: While Ca2+ wave incidence initially increased following isoproterenol application, this reversed after 60 min as wave frequency was reduced by ~30%.
source: Indeed, while we observed an expected initial increase in Ca2+ wave incidence following isoproterenol application, this reversed after 60 min as wave frequency was reduced by ~30% (Figure 4m).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4m.

claim: RyR cluster configuration was observed to have a large impact on spark fidelity in the mathematical model.
source: With baseline model parameters, RyR cluster configuration was observed to have a large impact on spark fidelity.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The solid CRU arrangement reproducibly generated full sparks, and thus spark fidelity was high.
source: Indeed, the solid CRU arrangement reproducibly generated full sparks, and thus spark fidelity was high (Figure 5b, top panels, Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: More quarks and failed sparks were observed in the CRUs with minor and moderate RyR dispersion.
source: However, more quarks and failed sparks were observed in the CRUs with minor and moderate RyR dispersion, and in the CRU with major fragmentation, no full Ca2+ sparks were generated.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: In the CRU with major fragmentation, no full Ca2+ sparks were generated.
source: However, more quarks and failed sparks were observed in the CRUs with minor and moderate RyR dispersion, and in the CRU with major fragmentation, no full Ca2+ sparks were generated.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: Spark fidelity declined steadily with increased fragmentation.
source: Indeed, spark fidelity declined steadily with increased fragmentation (95% CI in solid CRU: 28.6–37.8% vs. majorly fragmented CRU: 0–1.2%, Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Increasing channel sensitivity and Ca2+ release flux in the model increased the likelihood that dispersed CRU configurations successfully triggered Ca2+ sparks.
source: However, β-AR stimulation, as performed in experiments, augments both RyR sensitivity and, particularly at early stages, SR Ca2+ content. Increasing channel sensitivity and Ca2+ release flux accordingly in the model increased the likelihood that dispersed CRU configurations successfully triggered Ca2+ sparks (Figure 5b, bottom panels, Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: Although total Ca2+ released from a given CRU decreased with greater fragmentation, the proportion of leak that is silent increased dramatically.
source: Due to declining spark fidelity, we observed that although total Ca2+ released from a given CRU decreased with greater fragmentation, the proportion of leak that is silent increased dramatically.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5d.

claim: When including the effects of β-AR stimulation, the ratio of silent leak was strongly reduced for the mildly to moderately fragmented CRUs.
source: When including the effects of β-AR stimulation, the ratio of silent leak was strongly reduced for the mildly to moderately fragmented CRUs.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5d.

claim: For the majorly fragmented CRU, there remained a considerable amount of silent leak linked to partial activation of the CRU.
source: For the majorly fragmented CRU, however, there remained a considerable amount of silent leak (majorly fragmented w/β-AR: 37.5% silent leak, Figure 5d) linked to partial activation of the CRU (Ca2+ quarks).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Minor to moderate degrees of RyR dispersion had rather little impact on spark amplitude.
source: Minor to moderate degrees of RyR dispersion had rather little impact on spark amplitude, and simulated β-AR stimulation similarly increased spark magnitude for these CRUs (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Only majorly fragmented CRUs exhibited smaller Ca2+ sparks reflecting partial activation of RyRs.
source: Only majorly fragmented CRUs exhibited smaller Ca2+ sparks reflecting partial activation of RyRs.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The time to peak (TTP) of sparks increased with the degree of dispersion in the model.
source: The time to peak (TTP) of sparks increased with the degree of dispersion in our model (Figure 5f), and, under simulated β-AR activation, this was primarily due to the sensitized RyRs' improved ability to sustain regenerative release between clusters.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Western blotting revealed no significant change in total RyR expression in HF compared to sham.
source: Western blotting revealed no significant change in total RyR expression and only a tendency toward increased PKA phosphorylation at S2808 (Figure 6a and b, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 6a and b.

claim: Phosphorylation at S2814 was significantly increased by ~55% in HF.
source: However, phosphorylation at S2814 – a site linked to CaMKII activation – was significantly increased by ~55% in HF (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 6a and b.

claim: 3D dSTORM imaging revealed significant RyR dispersion in failing cells.
source: 3D dSTORM imaging of Sham and HF cardiomyocytes (Figure 6c) revealed significant RyR dispersion in failing cells, manifested at both the cluster level (Figure 6d; sham: 7.93 ± 0.46 vs. HF: 5.16 ± 0.27 RyRs/cluster) and CRU level (Figure 6e; sham: 20.79 ± 1.09 vs. HF: 14.82 ± 1.01 RyRs/CRU).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6c, d, and e.

claim: Inhibiting CaMKII phosphorylation with AIP in HF cells restored RyR organization to sham values.
source: Indeed, inhibiting CaMKII phosphorylation with AIP in HF cells restored RyR organization to sham values, as evidenced by a 49% increase in cluster size and a 47% increase in CRU size (Figure 6d and e).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6d and e.
